subject: mathematics
question_text: Use mathematical induction to prove that 4³ + 8³ + 12³ + … up to n terms = 16n²(n + 1)².

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.30, chapter 4 MATHEMATICAL INDUCTION, Short Answer question 10. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The split gives one mark to each of the four moves an induction proof is marked on — the base case, the hypothesis, the inductive step and the closing appeal to the principle — and leaves the opening statement step unmarked, matching every other card in this chapter. The nth term is read off the printed pattern as (4n)³, which reproduces 4³, 8³, 12³ at n = 1, 2, 3 and gives the stated sum 16n²(n+1)² at n = 1 (64) and n = 2 (576); that reading is ours, since the book states only the first three terms. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B prints eight short answers of which the student writes any six, each worth 4 marks, and Mathematical Induction supplies one of them on almost every paper. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this by induction — the nth term, and what comes out as a common factor in the third step.

steps.label: Find the nth term
steps.margin_note: Unmarked setup at 4 marks. The bases go 4, 8, 12, so they are multiples of 4 — the nth term is (4n)³, not 4n³.

recall.must_convey: That the bases are the multiples of 4, so the nth term is (4n)³, which is 64n³.
accept: the bases go four eight twelve so they are four n and the nth term is four n all cubed
general term is four n whole cubed which is sixty four n cubed
each base is a multiple of four so cube four n
nth term four n whole cube ani rastam

steps.why: Everything in this question follows from seeing that the bases are 4n. Once the term is 64n³, the series is 64 times the sum of cubes, which is why the answer is 64 × n²(n+1)²/4 = 16n²(n+1)².
common_mistakes: Writing the nth term as 4n³ instead of (4n)³, which drops a factor of 16.
Reading the bases as 4, 8, 12 but forgetting they are all cubed.
steps.memory_tip: The nth term is (4n)³ = 64n³, so this is just 64 times the sum of cubes: 64 × n²(n+1)²/4 = 16n²(n+1)².

steps.label: Check S(1)
steps.margin_note: One mark. Work out BOTH sides separately at n = 1 and say they are equal.
lines: ∴ L.H.S = R.H.S, so S(1) is true.

recall.must_convey: That at n = 1 the left side is 4 cubed, which is 64, and the right side is 16 times 1 times 4, which is also 64.
accept: left side is four cubed which is sixty four and right side is sixteen into one into four which is sixty four
put n equals one in both sides and both come to sixty four
the first case gives sixty four on each side
n equals one pettina rendu sides sixty four vasthai

steps.why: Landing on 64 from both sides is a good sign the nth term was read as (4n)³ and not 4n³. At n = 2 both sides give 576, which is a second check worth doing in rough work.
common_mistakes: Asserting S(1) is true without working out both sides.
steps.memory_tip: At n = 1 both sides give 64. At n = 2 both give 576: 64 + 512 and 16 × 4 × 9.

steps.label: Assume S(k) is true
steps.margin_note: One mark. Assume it for ONE value k and number the line (1) — Step 3 quotes that number.
lines: Step 2 — assume S(k) is true, k ∈ N

recall.must_convey: That S(k) is assumed true for some k in N — the sum up to (4k)³ equals 16k²(k+1)² — and the line is numbered (1).
accept: assume the sum up to four k cubed is sixteen k squared into k plus one squared
suppose s of k holds and call that equation one
take it as true for one value k in the naturals and number the line
k ki true ani assume chesi equation one ga rastam
reject: let it be true for k
then I assume s of k

steps.why: This is the assumption the method rests on. It is granted for one value only, and Step 3 has to earn the right to pass it on to the next value.
common_mistakes: Assuming the statement for ALL k, which assumes what is being proved.
Not numbering the line, so Step 3 cannot cite it.
steps.memory_tip: Replace n by k everywhere, last term (4k)³ and right side 16k²(k+1)². Number the line (1).

steps.label: Show S(k+1) follows
steps.margin_note: One mark, and the longest step on the page. The next term is 64(k+1)³. Take 16(k+1)² out and the bracket becomes a perfect square.
lines: Add it to both sides of (1):
So S(k+1) is true whenever S(k) is true.

recall.must_convey: That the next term is 64(k+1)³, that 16(k+1)² comes out as a common factor, and that k² + 4k + 4 is (k+2)², giving the formula with n replaced by k+1.
accept: the next term is sixty four into k plus one cubed and sixteen into k plus one squared comes out as a common factor
what is left is k squared plus four k plus four which is k plus two squared
take the common factor out and you get sixteen k plus one squared k plus two squared
next term add chesi common factor teeste k plus two squared vasthundi
reject: I show s of k plus one

steps.why: The added term 64(k+1)³ shares 16(k+1)² with the assumed sum, because 64 = 16 × 4. What is left inside is k² + 4k + 4, which is (k+2)² — exactly the bracket the formula needs at k+1.
common_mistakes: Writing the next term as 4(k+1)³ instead of [4(k+1)]³ = 64(k+1)³.
Expanding everything instead of factorising, which leaves a quartic that will not simplify.
Stopping before writing = R.H.S, so the step does not show what was asked.
steps.memory_tip: 64 = 16 × 4, so 16(k+1)² comes out and leaves k² + 4k + 4, which folds into (k+2)².

steps.label: Conclude by P.M.I
steps.margin_note: The last mark is for naming the principle. One sentence, one full mark.
lines: Hence, by the principle of finite

recall.must_convey: That S(1) is true and S(k) implies S(k+1), so by the principle of mathematical induction the result holds for every natural number n.
accept: since s of one is true and s of k gives s of k plus one by the principle of mathematical induction it holds for all n
hence by p m i the statement is true for every natural number
the base case and the inductive step together give it for all n in n
p m i prakaram anni natural numbers ki true

steps.why: The earlier steps prove two single statements — one about n = 1 and one about a step. Only the principle turns them into a claim about every n.
common_mistakes: Writing only 'hence proved' and never naming the principle.
Claiming it for all real numbers instead of all n ∈ N.
steps.memory_tip: The closing sentence names the principle and is worth a full mark on its own.
